concepts.title: Sanchi Stupa: Structure and Preservation
concepts.definition: The Sanchi stupas raised hemispherical domes (anda) over relics, crowned by a harmika, yashti and chhatra, ringed by stone railings with carved gateways (toranas); the site survived because nineteenth-century scholars like John Marshall documented it and the Begums of Bhopal protected it from treasure hunters.
concepts.key_idea: Sanchi is both a Buddhist monument and a modern conservation story: what survived was partly chosen by scholarship and patronage.

concepts.title: Sculpture and Symbols of the Buddha
concepts.definition: Early Buddhist art showed the Buddha aniconically - through an empty seat, a wheel, a pair of footprints or a lotus - while Jataka stories and scenes from his life filled the panels; anthropomorphic images of the Buddha appeared later, notably in the Mathura and Gandhara schools.
concepts.key_idea: The shift from symbols to figures tracks a change in devotion: from remembering the teacher to visualising him.

solution_steps.explain: empty seat, wheel and footprints stood for the Buddha's presence

concepts.title: Buddhist and Jain Traditions and Sects
concepts.definition: The chapter follows the Buddha's quest from householder to enlightened teacher, the sangha of monks and nuns open to all, and rival traditions like Jainism with its strict ahimsa and its digambara and svetambara split, alongside ajivikas and brahmanical sects - every group competing through buildings, texts and patronage.
concepts.key_idea: Religious competition was architectural: stupas, monasteries and cave shrines publicised each tradition's claims.

concepts.title: Reading Religious Buildings Historically
concepts.definition: Religious buildings are read as historical sources: donor inscriptions name kings, guilds, monks and ordinary women; the placement of stupas along routes shows their public role; and comparing plans across sites reconstructs the spread of ideas.
concepts.key_idea: Every carved pillar is an archive: donor lists at Sanchi record women, monks, kings and artisans of a whole society.
